title: My soul doth magnify (Luke 1:46–55)
hookLine: Mary's song turns the world over: the proud scattered, the hungry filled
tomorrow: and the man in this story who never says a single word…
last: GO TO THE ONE WHO UNDERSTANDS.

cards: You've seen the post: a team captioning the trophy photo the night before the final. Bold. Maybe a jinx.

Mary does something stranger. Blessed in Elizabeth's doorway, she answers with a song, and the song says God has already done things that, that day, plainly hadn't happened yet. He hath put down the mighty.
He hath filled the hungry. The mighty were still on their thrones. So why sing it in the past tense?

teach.b: Start with the first line, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "My soul doth magnify the Lord. And my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour."

In Latin the first word is Magnificat, and that's been the song's name for many centuries. To magnify is to make bigger, like a magnifying glass: not making God bigger than he is, but big enough to see.
Clue one comes next. God "hath regarded the humility of his handmaid." That part really had happened, to a young woman from a town in Galilee called Nazareth.
She starts from what God has already done for her. Clue two: the song is full of an older one.
Line by line it echoes the prayer of Hannah in the book of Samuel, another woman given a child against the odds, who sang that the full hire themselves out for bread and the hungry are filled.
Mary sings in her people's old words, about a God who has done this before.

teach.h: CLUE ONE: HE HATH REGARDED ME.
teach.b: Then: "He hath put down the mighty from their seat, and hath exalted the humble. He hath filled the hungry with good things; and the rich he hath sent empty away."
One way to put the clues together: the past tense reads less like a forecast and more like trust.
The Church sings or says it every evening, as the high point of Evening Prayer in the Liturgy of the Hours, so the promise goes out again each night: the lowly are lifted.

how: The Magnificat is sung or said every evening at Vespers, Evening Prayer in the Liturgy of the Hours, usually standing and making the sign of the cross as it begins.

games.q: what's inside the song — tap the pairs.
p: sang the older song Mary echoes

s: the Magnificat is a gentle lullaby
it's a song about the world upside down: the mighty put down, the hungry filled.
Mary's song is a prediction, written in the future tense
it's past tense: hath put down, hath filled. sung as if already done.
Mary's song echoes Hannah's prayer in the book of Samuel
another woman given a child against the odds, singing about the hungry filled.

games.q: a friend reads "he hath filled the hungry" and says, "but people are still hungry, so the song is wrong." which reply fits the lesson?
o: it's about the far future, so it can't be wrong yet.
it was only about Mary's own family, not the hungry.
it's sung as trust in what God has done before, not a news report.
games.why: Mary starts from what God already did for her, and borrows Hannah's song about a God who did it before. the past tense is trust.

practice: Read it out loud, at speaking volume, not in your head: Luke chapter one, verses forty-six to fifty-five, or just the first line, my soul doth magnify the Lord. Lean a little on the verbs: hath put down, hath exalted, hath filled.
Notice what it's like to say something in the past tense that the world is still waiting for.

wordCard.voice: Magnificat. Latin for magnifies: Mary's song, sung as if the lifting were already done.

orig.note: Latin: my soul magnifies the Lord. the first words gave the song its name.

carryVoice: Carry this: the lowly are lifted, in Mary's song and in Hannah's before her. Day twenty-three, done.
